ad_text: Aurora's POV The sexy lingerie clung to my skin; the mirror reflected my exposed, almost bursting breasts. I shifted on the bed, adjusting the lingerie I'd spent three hours picking out at the boutique downtown. The saleswoman had called it "a wearable love potion" and "battle armor that keeps a man in bed." I'd laughed, swiping the black card without hesitation. Enzo and I just needed a spark to repair the distance that had crept between us these past few months. Enzo ran a powerful crime family and was so busy I almost never saw him. The last time I'd slept with him was three months ago. The candles flickered on the nightstand. I'd cooked his favorite meal — bistecca alla fiorentina, seared rare with rosemary, the way his mother used to make it in the old country before she passed. There was a bottle of Barolo from his family's private cellar breathing on the table, and tucked in the drawer beside me was a collection of toys I'd never had the courage to buy before. Over these five years, as his Donna, I had developed a keen intuition. A vague sense of unease filled my heart, but I still decided to trust him. He'll be home soon, I told myself. He promised. But eight o'clock came and went. Nine. Ten. I checked my phone again. No messages. No calls. Just the same message I'd sent hours ago, still showing as "read" with no reply. Happy anniversary, Enzo. I have a surprise for you. Come home early? The steak had gone cold. The candles had burned down to stubs. I was feeling extremely anxious inside. To relieve this negative mood, I decided to look for a distraction. I opened Instagram and typed his name into the search bar. His account was set to private. Enzo valued his image as Don of the Crimson family, and he controlled every aspect of his public presence the way he controlled his territory. But tonight, someone had tagged him in a post. @Sophielove: The most magical birthday! Thank you for making my son's dreams come true. My thumb hovered over the screen. Don't click it. Don't— I clicked. The first photo showed a well-lit amusement park, the kind of place that gets rented out entirely, gates closed to the public, security in dark suits standing at every entrance. The second showed fireworks exploding over a carousel. And the third— My breath stopped. Enzo stood in a kitchen, flour dusted across his black shirt, the camera focused on his face, revealing a smile, his deep eyes curving into a gentle arc, as a little boy with dark curls held up a mixing bowl. I'd never seen Enzo like this before. Warm, peaceful, even adorable. I'd seen him ruthlessly decisive amidst gunfire, but I'd never seen him with such a warm smile. I struggled to shift my gaze. A woman stood beside them, her hand resting on Enzo's arm with the easy familiarity of someone who had never been told the rules. They were making a birthday cake together, like a family. The caption read: My two favorite boys. Five years old and already ruling the world. Five years old. We'd been married for five. My phone slipped from my fingers, clattering against the hardwood floor. The sound echoed through the empty bedroom, through the empty house I'd spent years turning into a home. No. No, this couldn't be right. Enzo was difficult, yes. Distant, often. Cold in the way men who order executions before breakfast learn to be. But he wasn't a cheater. He'd made me one vow at that altar, in front of both our families, in front of every capo on the East Coast. He wasn't the kind of man who would— Call him, my instinct urged. There has to be an explanation. I picked up my phone with trembling hands and dialed his number. "Hello?" The voice that answered wasn't his. It was soft, feminine, and a little breathless, like she'd been laughing. "Hello?" she said again. "Enzo, I think someone's calling you—oh, he just stepped out with Ethan. They're doing the sparklers. Can I take a message?" In the background, I heard a child's voice. "Daddy, look! Look what I can do!" Daddy. I froze. "Hello? Are you still there?" I couldn't speak. The call ended. I didn't know if I hung up or if she did. It didn't matter. I walked downstairs like a ghost. The dining room looked absurd: the crystal glasses, the cloth napkins folded into swans, the flowers I'd arranged just so. I picked up the platter of steak and dumped it into the trash. Everything else followed. Then I stood in the middle of the living room and looked at what I'd built. The curtains were sage green, because Enzo once mentioned his childhood home in the old country had green curtains. The ferns by the window were his favorite, even though I had to mist them twice daily to keep them alive in this climate. The walls held framed oil paintings of the old family estate at dusk. These were anniversary gifts I'd commissioned from artists he admired, back when I still believed anniversaries meant something to him. Our wedding photo hung above the fireplace. Enzo in his tailored black suit, me in white silk, our hands clasped on the cathedral steps as both families and their guests celebrated the union of two Mafia dynasties. He wasn't smiling in the picture. Enzo rarely smiled. But his eyes were soft, focused entirely on me. I'd stared at that photo a thousand times, searching for proof that our arrangement had become something real. That he loved me. Now it just looked like evidence of my own stupidity. I didn't know how long I sat in the dark bedroom, tears flowing and drying up again and again, until I heard the front door open, and a second later, he walked into the bedroom. He was still in his business suit, though the jacket was gone and his sleeves were rolled up, revealing the family tattoo on his wrist. His broad shoulders filled out his shirt, the holster strap cutting across his chest. His hair was loosely and carelessly styled, and under the light, shadows fell across his sharply defined face. As he walked in, he was as handsome as I remembered. Maybe even more. I caught the faintest trace of sugar and smoke clinging to his skin from birthday cake and fireworks. "You're still up," he said, loosening his tie. "I thought you'd be asleep." "It's our anniversary." He stopped short, like he'd just remembered. "I'm sorry, business ran late. I'll make it up to you tomorrow. We can go to that restaurant you like." A casual apology. After standing me up. As if I were an associate he'd kept waiting, not his wife. He started toward the bathroom, then stopped again. He turned, and his eyes zeroed in on my body, noticing the lingerie. His eyes were fixed on me, like a hunter fixing on moving prey. Intense desire swirled in his pupils. "Is this my surprise?" He stepped closer, his hand reaching for my waist. His movements were steady and powerful, allowing no room for refusal. He kissed down my neck and a little moan escaped me before he brought his lips down on mine. My brain flashed with images of him with his first love. Her hand on his arm. Flour on his shirt. I flinched away. Enzo froze. In five years of marriage, I'd never pulled away from him. Never rejected his touch. No one in this city rejected Enzo Thawthorne. His eyes revealed displeasure. "What's wrong with you?" "Where were you tonight?" "I told you. Business." "You weren't handling business." His expression shuttered closed. This was the Don's face, It was the cold mask he wore when he killed, revealing no emotion. "You're being paranoid." "I tried to call you, but some woman picked up—" My throat closed around the word. "You're overreacting." His voice turned cold, the voice that made grown men in his organization go pale. "Now come to bed and stop making this into something it isn't." "I'm not—" His phone rang. He answered without hesitation. Without even glancing at me. "Sophie? Slow down. What happened?" I watched his face transform. The coldness that belonged to the Don was replaced by an unusual tenderness. In five years of marriage, I had never received such favor from him. "It's okay," he murmured into the phone. "I'll be right there. Just stay calm. You're safe, no one touches you while you're under my protection." He hung up and grabbed his jacket from the chair, checking the gun at his side out of pure habit. "Enzo—" "Go to sleep," he said without looking at me. "We'll talk tomorrow." The door slammed behind him. A moment later, the engine of the Maybach roared out of the driveway. He left. On our anniversary. For his first love. The idea crushed me. My stomach twisted and I rushed into the bathroom. Bile surged up my throat, and I knelt over the toilet, choking as I vomited up what little I'd eaten today. My eyes watered, my forehead pressed against the porcelain as the nausea clawed through me again. Why am I throwing up? Could I be…? No. Impossible. We'd used contraceptives last time. Besides, this felt like normal nausea from not eating… right? Chapter 2 Aurora's POV I didn't sleep a wink all night. Every time I closed my eyes, I imagined Enzo and that woman lying in bed. But I could only lie there, staring at the ceiling, waiting for the sound of his car pulling into the driveway. However, the car never did. At three in the morning, I had checked my phone forty-seven times, finally accepting what my intuition had been telling me for hours. He wasn't coming back. In five years of marriage, Enzo had never left me for a single night. Not once. Even in the fiercest turf wars, even after late-night negotiations with the other family, even when he had a three-hour drive home, he always came back. He would crawl into bed, smelling of coffee and exhaustion, hold me in his arms, and fall asleep with his face buried in my hair. I used to think there must be a reason. Now I understood. What brought him home wasn't love, but responsibility. It was this sense of responsibility that made him marry me in the first place. The Don kept his promise. But Sophie came back, and duty was far from enough to overcome the feelings she evoked in him. I buried my face in the pillow and screamed until my voice was hoarse. The phone rang. I grabbed it, thinking he might be calling to explain, to apologize, to tell me it was all a misunderstanding. It was my father. "Aurora," his voice was hoarse. "It's your mother. She had a heart attack. We're at St. Michael's Hospital." The world seemed to stand still. "I'm coming right away." I immediately got up and ran. I ran all the way down the hospital corridor before stopping. My father was waiting for me outside the ICU. He looked haggard—this man who once commanded hundreds of people was now pacing the hospital corridor in a rumpled coat. "She's stable," he said before I could speak. "The doctors said she'll be fine." I collapsed into his arms, and he caught me, steadying me like he did when I was a child. "What happened?" "She was cleaning this morning and then she fell." His voice choked with emotion. "If I hadn't been there—" "But you were." I gripped his arm tightly. "She'll be alright." He nodded, but his eyes were vacant. We weren't the same people we were before. We'd lost everything. Our families were slaughtered by rival gunmen, our territory was taken over, our people scattered—some joined other families, others were buried in nameless graves. Although my parents received better treatment thanks to Enzo's support, the enormous disparity left my father often anxious. When the doctor finally allowed us to see her, she was awake. Her eyes immediately met mine, her face filled with guilt. "Oh, baby. I'm so sorry." "Mom, no—" "Your wedding anniversary." She reached out and grabbed my hand. "I ruined your wedding anniversary. You should be with Enzo, not stuck here with me." Mentioning his name sent another sharp pain through my chest. "You didn't mess anything up," I said, forcing a smile. "Enzo understands. He's just busy with family matters." My mother scrutinized my face. Married to a mob boss for thirty years, she was a master of social maneuvering, with a shrewdness she'd used to survive at the negotiating table all those years. "Aurora, what's wrong?" "Nothing." I squeezed her hand. "I was just worried about you." She didn't believe me, but she was too weak to press for answers, and I was too exhausted to be honest. So we sat in silence, her thumb circling my palm, both pretending everything was normal. That afternoon, Enzo arrived. The hospital director greeted him at the door. I watched them shake hands through the window; the director almost bowed respectfully. Of course. Enzo wasn't just any mob boss. He was the head of the Crimson family, one of the most powerful criminal organizations on the East Coast. Half of the hospital's newly built cardiology building was constructed with money from the Crimson family, laundered through three charitable foundations. His word could decide a person's fate. Within minutes, my mother was moved to the hospital's best suite. A group of specialists suddenly appeared, vying to assure Enzo that his mother-in-law would receive the best care. "Your son-in-law is fantastic," a nurse whispered to my father. "You're so lucky to have him." My father beamed with pride. I wanted to scream. None of them knew. What they saw was a powerful mob boss, a generous husband, a dutiful son-in-law. What they couldn't see was that last night, while his wife waited alone, he had spent the night in another woman's bed. Enzo approached me, deliberately maintaining a calm expression. "Are you alright?" "Fine." He frowned. "You look tired. Did you sleep?" Did I sleep? I almost laughed out loud. "I'm worried about my mother." He nodded, took a step closer, and gently placed his hand on my waist. It was his usual caress. I saw a relieved smile on my mother's face. Perhaps she believed that even though this marriage was fraught with self-interest, her daughter would still be happy. But alas, Mother, things didn't go as planned. Enzo married me not out of love, but as part of an arrangement. The Serrano family's attack nearly wiped out my family, and my father chose to marry me into Enzo's family to ensure my safety. I knew all this all along. But Enzo and I had grown up together. We had played in the same garden of the old manor, trained with the same soldiers at the same shooting range, and attended the same family gatherings—baptisms, banquets, funerals. On our wedding day, he looked at me, and I thought I saw genuine affection in his eyes. What a fool I was. The return of his first love shattered all my illusions. Sophie returned, and her return was proof of where Enzo's true feelings lay. "Aurora?" Enzo's voice pierced my thoughts. "Are you sure you're alright?" I turned to face him, but froze. Just below his shirt collar was a pink lipstick mark. He'd actually come to the hospital wearing her lipstick. To play the role of a considerate husband in front of my family, he'd even skipped a shower. I smelled a faint scent of another woman's perfume, and my stomach churned. That pink lipstick mark mocked everything between us like a ghost. The vows we exchanged in front of our families, my ten-year-long crush on the boy from the neighboring estate, and our five years of so-called marital bliss—all so fragile, shattered by a single lipstick mark. "I'm sorry," I stammered, then fled into the bathroom. I vomited as soon as I reached the toilet. I threw up everything, and only one thought occupied my mind: Divorce. Chapter 3 Aurora's POV I stood at the front desk, my heart hammering as the clerk slid a thick envelope across the counter. The brass plaque behind her read Castellan & Associates — Family Counsel, Contracts & Dissolutions. The law firm that had served both our families for three generations. The firm that had drafted my marriage contract. "Mrs. Crimson?" The clerk peered at me over her glasses. "Is everything alright?" "Fine." I tore the seal open with my thumb and eased the papers out just far enough to read the header. Petition for Dissolution of Marriage Contract — Preliminary Draft My heart sank. The form was blank, waiting for signatures and dates. Waiting to undo an alliance two families had bled for. I folded it back into the envelope, smoothing the crease with shaking fingers. "Thank you." I tucked the envelope into my bag. I turned to leave and walked straight into a familiar chest. "Aurora?" Mark. Enzo's Underboss and one of my oldest friends. We'd grown up together in the same circle of family children, back when Blackthorne and Crimson were separate territories with their own politics. His eyes dropped to the bag I was clutching against my chest. "What are you doing here?" "Nothing." The lie slipped out. "Just… my mother's medical bills." Mark frowned. "How is your mother?" "Much better. She should be discharged in a few days." "That's good." He hesitated, then added, "I hope you're doing well." My smile shattered like broken glass. "I'm fine." "Hmm." Mark gently squeezed my shoulder, his touch warm and familiar. "It was nice to see you, Aurora. Take care of yourself." I nodded and slipped past him. I had to get ready for dinner. Enzo was treating me to dinner at his favorite restaurant to make up for our missed anniversary. The restaurant was beautiful. Crystal chandeliers, white tablecloths, and a string quartet playing softly in the corner. Enzo had reserved a private room overlooking the city skyline, and they even had $500 bottles of wine. This was exactly the kind of place he always chose. To show the world that the Don of the Crimson family would go to any lengths for his Donna. But this wasn't my favorite restaurant. My favorite was a small Italian restaurant downtown, with red checkered tablecloths, where all the dishes were cooked by an elderly Italian lady. Enzo took me there once a few years ago, and I told him it was the best meal I'd ever had. He never took me there again. "I brought you something," Enzo said, pushing a velvet box across the table. Before even opening it, I knew what was inside. A diamond and white gold bracelet. Exactly the same style he'd given me for our anniversaries for the past five years. "It's beautiful," I said, as I always do. I used to proudly wear every bracelet, showing them off to the ladies of other families at every grand event. These were gifts from my husband, and I always tried to convince myself they were an expression of his love. Now I understood. He didn't understand me at all. He just had his assistant order the same thing year after year, because it was much easier than figuring out my true preferences. I knew him inside and out. His favorite color (navy blue). His favorite food (the braised beef his mother had brought from her hometown, which had taken me months to recreate). He liked his coffee black. His right hand instinctively reached for his holster when a stranger moved too quickly. He didn't even know I was allergic to matcha. A waitress brought dessert, a delicate green cake sprinkled with matcha powder. "Matcha cake," she announced. "This was specially prepared by the chef for the occasion." I stared at the cake, remembering the photos on Instagram, my throat tightening. Enzo had made a cake for the person he truly loved. And for me, he'd had a stranger's chef make this thing that could land me in the hospital. "What's wrong?" Enzo asked. Everything was wrong. "I can't eat this," I whispered. "I'm allergic to matcha." "When did it start?" "Always, Enzo." He gestured for the waiter to take the cake away, but it was too late. We'd been married five years, and he didn't even know about such a basic allergy. I couldn't breathe. "I have to go." I jumped up, the chair scraping against the floor. He grabbed my arm. "Aurora, wait—" My bag slipped from my shoulder and fell to the floor. Things were scattered everywhere—lipstick, keys, wallet, and a thick envelope from Castellan's office. Enzo bent down to help me gather my things. His fingers had just touched the envelope when his phone rang. He glanced at the screen. "I have to take this." He was already walking towards the door. "Go home. I'll see you there." "Enzo—" But he was already gone, phone to his ear, his voice low and gentle, disappearing around the corner. His driver didn't even glance back at me. The envelope was left forgotten on the floor. I made the only sensible choice: I hailed a taxi and followed him. I knew it was ridiculous—the Donna of the Crimson family tailing her husband's Maybach through rush-hour traffic like a second-rate private investigator. But I wanted answers. The taxi took me to St. Michael's Hospital. My mother was recovering there. I walked down the familiar corridor, my stomach churning. I followed in Enzo's wake, past staff who nodded respectfully and hurried to open doors for him—trailing after him like a lovesick fool. I found him in the pediatric ward. Through the window of a private room, I saw my husband holding another woman. Sophie cried, burying her face in his chest. On the bed behind them, a little boy slept, an IV drip attached to his small hand. "It's just a fever," he whispered, stroking her hair. "He'll be alright, I promise." "I'm so scared," Sophie's voice trembled. "When he started having the fever, I didn't know what to do. I just… I need you." "I'm here now." He kissed her forehead. "I'll always be here." A sharp, agonizing pain shot through me. I remembered that night I told Enzo I wanted a child. We'd been married for two years, and I felt it was time. I brought it up while Enzo was still inside me. The next morning, he handed me a box of emergency contraceptive pills and watched me swallow them. "We're not ready," he said. And then the discussion ended. His word was final. I thought he just didn't want children. But it turned out— He didn't want children with me. He wanted children with her. Sophie turned slightly to the side, reaching for a tissue on the bedside table. The light shone on her wrist. She was wearing the exact same bracelet as the one on my wrist, diamonds and white gold. My vision blurred, and I ripped off my own bracelet. The clasp cut my skin, drawing blood, but I didn't care. I threw the bracelet on the floor, watching it slide across the tiles like a worthless object. Because to him, I was worthless, easily replaceable. While he waited for the woman he truly loved, I was just a placeholder, a substitute named Donna. I didn't break down in tears until I got back to the taxi, the sobs making my whole body tremble. What remained of my heart curled up into a small, silent ball. I'll serve him the divorce papers after my mother is discharged from the hospital. Chapter 4 Enzo's POV The boy's fever subsided around midnight. I watched his small chest rise and fall, gradually calming down, the flush on his cheeks fading. Sophie finally stopped crying; she leaned on my shoulder, exhaustion making her drowsy. "Thank you," she whispered. "I don't know what I would have done without you." "You don't need to do anything." I gently brushed a strand of hair from her cheek. "I told you, I'm here." She smiled weakly and closed her eyes. It wasn't until I walked into the corridor of the private clinic that I remembered Aurora. I took out my phone and dialed her number. The number you dialed is unavailable. I frowned and dialed again. The result was the same. What happened? Aurora never turned off her phone. Even when she was angry with me, she always kept it on, waiting for me to call and apologize. This was her usual pattern: sulking, pouting, waiting for me to coax her into happiness. Aurora needed a man to comfort her; I was used to it. But this time, it seemed different. A sense of unease crept into my heart. Just as I was about to call again, my gaze was suddenly drawn to something on the floor. The bracelet—the one I'd given Aurora. I bent down to pick it up, examining it closely in my hand. The clasp was broken, bent at an odd angle, as if it had been forcefully ripped off. A chill ran down my spine. Had she been here? Had she seen us? "Enzo?" Sophie appeared in the doorway, her brow furrowed, her face full of worry. "Is everything alright?" I stuffed the bracelet into my pocket. "I'm fine. I have to go home." "Of course." She took a step closer, a hint of guilt flashing across her face. "I'm so sorry to have taken up so much of your time. Your wife must be angry with you." "Don't worry about it." I grabbed my coat and headed for the elevator. "Aurora isn't the kind of person who causes trouble. She knows her place." I drove straight home. When I arrived, the manor was pitch black. The guard at the gate nodded silently, gesturing for me to come in. I found Aurora in our bedroom, curled up on her side, her back to the door. The curtains were drawn. She didn't move when I entered. I frowned. What was wrong with her? I stood there, gazing at her thin shoulders for a long time. If she had seen me with Sophie at the clinic, she would have come at me immediately. That was the Aurora I knew. It was how she'd always been. If she sensed something was wrong, she'd keep asking until you said what she wanted to know. I slowly exhaled, the tension in my chest gradually dissipating. Aurora had always been a pampered little princess. She was the Blackthorne family's beloved only daughter, and everyone doted on her. If things didn't go her way, she'd throw a tantrum. She demanded attention as if it were her birthright. She loved passionately and expected an equally passionate response. I used to find her adorable. For example, if I forgot to bring her her favorite flowers, she'd pout; or she'd sulk for days over some perceived slight. When she looked at me with those hopeful eyes, I could easily forgive her bad temper. But if she found out the truth about Sophie and Ethan, if she found out about the child, and everything I'd been hiding, she'd make my life a living hell. I would never tolerate it. Aurora was my Donna, but she needed to understand that some things were beyond her control. Some things she could only accept. I sat on the edge of the bed and took out the bracelet. "Aurora." I gently patted her shoulder. "Wake up." I tried to help her put the bracelet on, but she immediately opened her eyes. I held up the bracelet. "Why did you leave this at the clinic?" She stared at the bracelet as if it were a venomous snake about to strike. "I lost it when I went to visit my mother." She had clearly discovered my secret. I waited for her to explode, but she remained calm. This unsettled me more than any of her outbursts. "Put it on." I reached for her wrist. She pulled away. "No." "Aurora." "I don't want to." Her voice choked. "It… it's nothing special. It's nothing." "Okay." I placed the bracelet on the bedside table, trying to sound patient. "I'll buy you a better one." She laughed, a laugh that stirred a dark and intense possessiveness within me. I reached for her again, my hand sliding down her waist. "Come here." I pulled her closer, my lips lightly brushing her neck. "Let me make it up to you." She pushed me away. "Stop." Her voice was hoarse. "Don't do this." "What's wrong with you? You've been acting crazy these past few days." I growled in a low voice. "Crazy?" She sat bolt upright, her eyes blazing with anger. "It's you…" My phone rang. We both froze. Sophie's name flashed on the screen. Aurora lunged for the phone. Instinctively, I grabbed her arm to stop her, but she turned her head and still reached for the phone, my grip stronger than I intended. She fell. She hit the ground hard — a dull thud, then a piercing scream. I stood there, stunned, unsure what to do. I wanted to go over and check if she was hurt, but then I remembered all her tantrums, all her attempts to play the victim and get her way. No, not this time. She needed to learn her lesson. This behavior was absolutely unacceptable. I took her in, gave her a home. She had to respect that, or face the consequences. I picked up the phone and walked out without looking back. Aurora's POV I lay on the cold floor, my buttocks throbbing from hitting the edge of the bedside table, the angle of my bent wrist making me nauseated. But more unbearable than the physical pain was the sound of his footsteps descending the stairs. He didn't even turn around, not once. My heart felt like it had been ripped open, a wound that would never heal. I tried to sit up, but my arms wouldn't obey me. Why? Why was I being treated like this? A clap of thunder startled me. My heart leaped. No— Lightning flashed across the night sky, and the power went out. Darkness swallowed everything. I screamed, or rather, tried to scream. The sound that came out was a suppressed gasp. I was alone, trapped in the darkness. I've always been afraid of storms. Ever since I was a child. Back then, enemy gunmen attacked our yard during a storm, using the thunder as cover. Enzo knew everything. He had been with me through countless storms. Where was he now? I fumbled for my phone, trembling, and dialed his number. The number you dialed is unavailable. I tried again. No response. "Please," I sobbed into the darkness. "Please, Enzo. Please come back. I'm so scared. Please." Another clap of thunder shook the windows. The phone slipped from my hand. Before the darkness engulfed me, my last sensation was that of a shattering heart, and I cried out for a husband who would never answer. Chapter 5 Aurora's POV The first thing I noticed was the sound. A slow, rhythmic beep pierced my unconsciousness. I slowly opened my eyes, but the blinding light stung my eyes, making me wince and immediately turn my head to the side. A chemical odor filled my nostrils, pulling me back up from the depths of unconsciousness. When my eyes finally adjusted to the light, I saw white walls, a tiled ceiling, and a buzzing fluorescent light overhead. My gaze fell on a transparent plastic tube winding down my arm. I was in the hospital, but I couldn't remember how I got here. Memories flooded back: thunder, torrential rain pounding on the roof, and the sudden fear that struck me before I collapsed onto the cold floor. "Enzo?" I whispered. Before losing consciousness, I had called him, praying he would come pick me up. A glimmer of hope lingered. He must have brought me here. He wouldn't abandon me; it was all a misunderstanding. We'll talk it out, clear up the misunderstanding, and everything will be back to normal. He loves me. A slight smile played on my lips. I tried to sit up, supporting myself with my palms, but a sharp pain shot through my wrist. "Ah!" I cried out. The door flung open, and a woman in surgical scrubs entered. She checked the monitor beside my bed and said softly, "You're in the intensive care unit. You collapsed from stress and exhaustion." I swallowed hard, trying to calm myself. Intensive Care Unit. I couldn't believe it; things were serious enough to require intensive care. "And… there's something else," the doctor continued, her voice almost gentle. "You're pregnant." My breath caught, the air in my lungs instantly vanishing. Pregnant? My thoughts instantly returned to the last time he touched me. My heart was pounding as I tried to recall if we had taken any safety precautions, but my memory wouldn't cooperate and was a jumbled mess. My throat tightened. "Did you... tell anyone else?" "No," the doctor replied immediately. "It's the patient's private information; no one else knows." A feeling of relief washed over me. I stroked my belly. The sudden arrival of this little life had left my mind blank. My first thought was of Enzo. Would he be happy? Just then, the doorknob clicked open. Someone entered the room. I held my breath, my heart pounding. A hope burned within me, both wild and desperate. Enzo. He brought me here. He cared about me. A smile returned to my face, but my lips trembled slightly. Until the figure appeared before me. It wasn't Enzo. It was Jenna, Enzo's sister. "My God," she whispered, sitting on the edge of my bed and taking my hand. "How are you feeling? I was terrified." My fragile hope shattered instantly. I had thought he would come to save me. I had even decided that if he showed up, I would forget everything that had happened and try to forgive him. But he disappointed me again. His absence was so suffocating. "Enzo isn't home," Jenna said softly, her gaze falling on our clasped hands. "I went to his house last night because he hadn't answered the phone. The power went out, and I found you lying on the floor." I slowly lowered my head. I realized I'd been abandoned on the cold floor like an insignificant object. A dull ache shot through my chest; Enzo's indifference felt like a dagger, twisting within me. I could barely breathe. "How long have I been unconscious?" I forced myself to speak, my gaze shifting between the doctor and Jenna. "We don't know," the doctor replied. "You're lucky you were brought here in time." Lucky? How could this be considered lucky? Waking up to find my husband had chosen someone else, while I lay dying in the darkness—was that lucky? Stroganoff, nå berømt i mange land, hadde sin opprinnelse i Russland på 1500-tallet, på Stroganov-palasset i St. Petersburg. I denne perioden utmerket den seg som en raffinert rett, med originaloppskriften bestående av terninger av filet mignon med rømme og sennep. Det var imidlertid ikke før den kommunistiske revolusjonen i 1917 at oppskriften spredte seg over hele Europa, brakt med av russiske eksil. Dermed nådde retten Frankrike, hvor den fikk versjoner med sopp, og ble til slutt populær på Maxim's, en av de mest kjente restaurantene i Paris. Over tid reiste stroganoff verden rundt og gjennomgikk en rekke tilpasninger i forskjellige land. Stroganoff ble introdusert til Brasil etter andre verdenskrig av den østerrikske immigranten Max von Stuckart, som ankom Rio de Janeiro på slutten av 1940-tallet. Max, som hadde jobbet på anerkjente europeiske restauranter, fant raskt sin plass på Copacabana Palace. I 1947 grunnla han den berømte nattklubben Vogue i Copacabana, hvor retten ble en fremtredende del av menyen. Stroganoff er ganske populær i Brasil og Portugal, hvor det finnes mange varianter, inkludert storfekjøtt, kylling eller reker. Hovedkarakteristikken ved brasiliansk stroganoff er bruken av tomatsaus eller ketchup blandet med fløte og sopp. Den serveres alltid med hvit ris og "palha poteter" ved siden av, mens den i Russland vanligvis serveres med kokte poteter. Stroganoff er også populær i Sverige og Norge. I Sverige er en vanlig variant pølsestroganoff, som bruker den tradisjonelle svenske pølsen kalt falukorv som kjøtterstatning.
